title: The musical Brunis family and Papa Lane's Reliance band
summary: Siblings' instruments, his father's after-dinner family sessions, and early dance jobs with Papa Lane.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Can you tell me some more about your home when you started? Your father and the rest of your family, what they played?
Well, there was Richard and my two late brothers Henry played trombone. My brother Rudy, he was the last one, Barrett. He was 70 years old. He played bass fiddle.
And Rudy was the oldest in the family.

Yeah. And he was a brewmeister. No, Richie's after, before. And Rudy was a brewmeister in the New Orleans Brewing Company. And then there was Henry, then there was Merritt, and there's Albert and myself, and my brother Richard, the four of us are living here. And my sister and my mother, they played guitar, both guitar and piano. And my old man would get us out after dinner and make us all. We had Abby, Merritt, and Richie on trumpets, and my brother Henry on the trombone, and I played the upright alto. I was playing the upright. That was my first instrument. When I saw Henry play the trombone, I drooled, and I threw the alto away and wanted to play trombone. And then my sister, my mother, and he'd get there with the violin, play the mockingbird when the maple leaves were falling, and we'd start playing so nice for a couple of, give me kicks, and we'd start jazzing up. He'd run the hell out of it and throw the violin down. He says, you little jazz damn fools, he says.
So did you really play out there almost every night on the-

Well, no. When he felt in the mood, if he didn't eat too much, he'd say, all right, boys, get the instruments, and we'd have to be there. And I'll guarantee you, it's not like today. At nine o'clock, we hung out when we were playing music. Papa Lane used to pick me up, see? I played with his Reliance band, and he'd pick me up and we'd play the dance, and we'd get fifty cents an hour, Crescent Park, Owls Halls, Suburban Park, Elvira Park, and Algiers, and we'd play the parades. But he'd pick me up, and he'd take me to the job, and if it was too far away from my house, I'd sleep at his house, see?

And then he'd bring me home the next day, and he'd give my mother the money, and my mother would give me a dime to go get a piece of candy or something. And at nine o'clock, and we weren't working, when that market bell rang, boy, I had to be in there at nine o'clock, he'd be behind the door, he'd bring us with a baseball bat. And there's seven of us, and thank God, there's none of us stepped outside the law in there. And the kids today, boy, we, I advise kids to take musical instruments up and keep away from those guns.
